title: Mishpatim: straight after Sinai, the details
hookLine: after the thunder come laws about workers, damages and loans
tomorrow: Mishpatim: the heart of a stranger (Exodus 23:9)

lines: BIG WORDS ON THE LOBBY WALL.
AFTER THE THUNDER, AN OPEN PIT.
cards: A hospital lobby often has big words on the wall: compassion, dignity, care. The words don't wash anyone's hands.

What carries them out is a laminated checklist by the sink, a chart at the foot of the bed, a nurse checking the name on a wristband twice. The big words live in the small print. The Torah works the same way.
One portion is full of thunder, lightning, a mountain on fire and the voice of God. The very next opens, almost without a pause, with laws about servants, injuries, a goring ox and an open pit.

teach.b: The portion's first verse, in the old Jewish translation: "Now these are the ordinances which thou shalt set before them." Ordinances, in Hebrew mishpatim: laws, judgments, the rules a court would use.
And they're astonishingly practical. A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year.
Dig a pit, leave it open, and an animal falls in: you pay. If your ox has gored before and you didn't keep it in, you're responsible. Lend money to a poor person, and don't charge interest.

Take a neighbor's cloak as a pledge, and give it back before sunset, because it's what they sleep in. Rashi, the medieval commentator, stops on the first word. In Hebrew it's not just these, it's and these.

teach.h: RASHI: AND THESE, ALSO FROM SINAI.
teach.b: That little and, he says, joins this portion to the one before: just as the Ten Words came from Sinai, so did these. For Rashi, the goring ox comes from the same place as the thunder.

He also notices set before them, and says it means like a table that's set, ready to eat from, everything laid out clearly. That's the point of the portion. Sinai wasn't meant to stay on the mountain.
It was meant to come down into the barn, the field, the loan, the paycheck.
Holiness here doesn't float. It shows up in the fine print.

how: The civil laws of Mishpatim are studied through the Talmud's tractates on damages and property, Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia and Bava Batra.

practice: Choose one small rule you usually treat as a nuisance: returning the shopping cart, paying someone on time, cleaning up after yourself at work, driving at the limit near a school.
Picture the person on the other end of it, the worker collecting carts, the contractor waiting for payment, the child crossing the street, and let the rule become a way of caring for them.
